qs.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with a painful mass around the knee region. An X-ray of the distal femur metaphysis shows periosteal elevation forming Codman's triangle and a sunburst pattern of spiculated new bone. What is the underlying nature of this tumor?
qs.e: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor, classically affecting the metaphysis of long bones like the distal femur with Codman's triangle and sunburst patterns. Benign tumors do not show these aggressive malignant periosteal reactions.
qs.s: Bone & Cartilage Tumors: Osteoma to Osteosarcoma Pathology — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A 10-year-old child presents with fever, bone pain, raised ESR, and a diaphyseal mass in the femur mimicking osteomyelitis. X-ray shows an 'onion skin' periosteal reaction. Cytogenetic testing will most likely reveal which translocation?
qs.e: Ewing's sarcoma is characterized by the t(11;22) translocation resulting in the EWS-FLI1 fusion gene and small round blue cells. This tumor predominantly affects the diaphysis of long bones in children.
qs.s: Bone & Cartilage Tumors: Osteoma to Osteosarcoma Pathology — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A 30-year-old female presents with pain and swelling near the knee joint. Radiography of the distal femur reveals a 'soap bubble' lytic expansile lesion that extends from the epiphysis to the articular surface after the growth plates have closed. What is the defining histological feature?
o: Multinucleated giant cells in mononuclear stroma
Small round blue cells forming dense sheets
Lobules of hyaline cartilage with calcification
qs.e: Giant cell tumor (osteoclastoma) is characterized microscopically by multinucleated giant cells scattered in a background of mononuclear stromal cells. Malignant osteoblasts producing woven bone are found in osteosarcoma.
qs.s: Bone & Cartilage Tumors: Osteoma to Osteosarcoma Pathology — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A 16-year-old adolescent is evaluated for a primary malignant bone tumor. The tumor is located in the metaphysis of the distal femur and displays a sunburst X-ray pattern. Which of the following best describes the direct histological product of this tumor's malignant cells?
o: Osteoid or woven bone directly formed
Sheets of small round blue cells
qs.e: Osteosarcoma cells are malignant osteoblasts that directly produce osteoid or woven bone. Hyaline cartilage lobules are produced by chondromas and chondrosarcomas.
qs.s: Bone & Cartilage Tumors: Osteoma to Osteosarcoma Pathology — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: An imaging modality is chosen to calculate bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine, hip, and proximal femur. Which imaging technique is standard for this purpose?
qs.e: DXA is the standard method used to calculate BMD at the lumbar spine, hip, and proximal femur. Quantitative ultrasonography has no radiation but is not as accurate as DXA.

qs.q: A 17-year-old boy presents with progressive knee pain, night pain, and a mixed lytic-blastic metaphyseal lesion of the distal femur with periosteal elevation forming a triangular shadow. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: A Codman triangle along with a mixed lytic-blastic metaphyseal lesion in an adolescent is the classic presentation of osteosarcoma. Ewing sarcoma typically presents with an onion-skin lamellated reaction rather than this specific metaphyseal mix.
qs.s: Bone & Soft Tissue Pathology: Cases, Tumors, & Answers — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A 5-year-old child presents with an acute hematogenous infection of the femur. Given the local vascular anatomy in this age group, where is the infection most likely to initially localize within the bone?
o: Metaphysis region of the long bone
Diaphysis cortex of the long bone
qs.e: In older children, pyogenic osteomyelitis most commonly localizes in the metaphysis due to local vascular loops that slow blood flow. In neonates, vessels cross the growth plate allowing involvement of both the metaphysis and epiphysis.
qs.s: Bone & Joint Pathology: Basic Structure, Cells, and Fractures — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A patient sustains a fracture of the neck of the femur and is informed of an increased risk of avascular necrosis. Which vessel group is primarily responsible for supplying the femoral head?
o: Retinacular vessels from the extracapsular arterial ring
Obturator artery branches from the acetabular notch
Descending genicular branches of the femoral artery
Internal pudendal artery branches via the lesser sciatic foramen
qs.e: The femoral head is supplied by retinacular vessels arising from an extracapsular arterial ring formed by the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries. Damage to these vessels during a femoral neck fracture leads to avascular necrosis.
qs.s: Anatomy Marathon 1 — Lower Limb — Revision Guide: MCQs

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The femur is the longest bone, forming the thigh and supporting weight. Its anatomy dictates joint mechanics, blood flow, and common injury patterns. Clinicians use this knowledge to diagnose fractures, assess vascular status, and plan surgeries.

sections.p: The femur is the largest and strongest bone, extending from the hip to the knee. It bears most of the body’s weight and provides attachment for major muscle groups.
It consists of a proximal head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, shaft, and distal condyles. The head articulates with the acetabulum, while the condyles meet the tibia.
Anteriorly lies the quadriceps tendon and patella; posteriorly the hamstrings. Medially and laterally, the femur is adjacent to the iliac crest and tibia.
The femoral artery gives off the profunda femoris and perforating branches. The nutrient artery enters the shaft, while the epiphyseal arteries supply the head and neck.

t.b: Details complex fractures and bone loss
Assesses soft tissue and vascular injury

sections.p: The femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh; the obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh; the sciatic nerve supplies the posterior thigh.
The femur allows hip flexion, extension, abduction, and rotation, and knee flexion and extension. It transfers weight from the pelvis to the lower limb.
Fractures of the neck, shaft, and distal femur are common. Avascular necrosis follows neck fractures. Osteolytic lesions may indicate metastases.
On exam, assess femoral pulse, capillary refill, and distal neurovascular status. A positive Trendelenburg sign suggests hip abductor weakness.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain with deformity, inability to bear weight, loss of distal pulses, or neuro deficits

faq.q: What causes avascular necrosis after a femoral neck fracture?
faq.a: Disruption of the medial circumflex femoral artery leads to bone death.

faq.q: How does a distal femur fracture present?
faq.a: Pain, swelling, and inability to extend the knee; the leg may be shortened.

faq.q: Why is the femur prone to osteolytic metastases?
faq.a: It has rich red marrow and venous plexus that allow tumor spread.

exam: Describe the blood supply to the femoral head and its clinical significance.
Explain how a femoral neck fracture can lead to avascular necrosis.
